title: Libra Philanthropies 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort: 9-Month Leadership Programme for Emerging Climate Leaders
summary: The Libra Philanthropies 2027 Rising Global Leaders (RGL) Changemakers Climate Cohort is now accepting applications from emerging leaders who are already working to advance climate action through community-based initiatives, organizations, or other climate-focused work. The programme is a nine-month leadership development and experiential learning initiative designed to help rising climate leaders strengthen their leadership capabilities, expand their networks, understand the systems shaping climate decisions, and build their ability to create meaningful change within their communities and beyond. Applications opened on September 22, 2026 , and will close on October 23, 2026 . The programme will run from January to September 2027 and will combine in-person convenings, online sessions, peer learning, strategic workshops, experiential learning, and individualized capacity-building support. What Is the 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort? The Climate Cohort is part of Libra Philanthropies Rising Global Leaders programme, which supports emerging and community-based leaders through leadership development, mentorship, immersive learning, peer exchange, and international networking opportunities. Within the Rising Global Leaders programme, the Changemakers pathway is designed for leaders who already have a clear focus area and are actively creating impact within their communities. The Climate Cohort applies this approach specifically to climate action and community-grounded climate work. The 2027 cohort recognizes that climate change affects much more than the environment. Climate-related decisions can influence: Where people can live How communities develop Economic growth and livelihoods Population displacement Wildlife and ecosystems Energy systems Land use Financial systems Public policy Community resilience Long-term development Libra Philanthropies programme is therefore intended to help emerging leaders better understand the systems, institutions, funding structures, and decision-making environments that influence climate action. Why the Climate Cohort Was Created One of the central ideas behind the programme is the gap between those who experience climate impacts most directly and those who participate in decisions about climate policy and investment . Climate decisions made today can have consequences that extend across generations. Yet emerging leaders who are closest to climate-related challenges may not always have access to the institutions, networks, resources, or decision-making spaces where priorities are established. The Climate Cohort seeks to help address this gap by providing participants with: Knowledge Leadership skills Networks Confidence Organizational capacity Exposure to climate decision-making systems Opportunities for peer learning Experiential learning Connections with other leaders The official programme describes the goal as helping emerging climate leaders navigate the systems influencing climate action and strengthen their ability to create change. Who Is the Climate Cohort Designed For? The programme is intended for climate leaders between the ages of 20 and 35 who are already leading or playing a significant role in a climate-focused initiative or organization. The initiative or organization should: Have been operating for at least one year Be nonpartisan Preferably have an annual budget below $500,000 Address climate change in ways grounded in the needs and experiences of the communities it serves Applicants should also be willing to collaborate, share their experiences, participate in collective learning, and contribute to a broader community of climate leaders. Importantly, the programme is intended for people who are already taking action , rather than individuals who are simply interested in climate change but have no existing climate-focused initiative or organizational role. What Participants Will Learn The 2027 Climate Cohort is organized around three thematic pillars . 1. Understanding the Climate System Participants will explore how different systems influence climate action. This includes examining: Funding Power Institutions Accountability Climate commitments Decision-making The relationship between resources and climate solutions The goal is to help participants understand not only what climate challenges exist, but also how decisions about climate solutions are made and which factors determine whether those solutions receive support . 2. Local Adaptation and Community Resilience The second pillar focuses on the relationship between climate change and people s everyday lives. Participants will examine: How climate change affects communities Community responses to climate challenges Locally led adaptation Resilience-building Community-based approaches to climate action This emphasis reflects the programme s focus on climate initiatives that are grounded in the needs and experiences of communities. 3. Moving From Participation to Climate Action and Influence The third pillar focuses on helping participants translate participation into sustained influence. Participants will develop relationships, strategies, tools, and credibility that can help them advance climate solutions and participate more effectively in spaces where climate priorities are shaped. This includes developing the ability to move from simply participating in climate conversations toward building meaningful influence and sustained action . What Does the 9-Month Programme Include? The Climate Cohort combines several different learning and leadership-development approaches. In-Person Convenings Participants will come together in person three times during the programme . Kickoff — February 2027 The programme begins with an in-person kickoff focused on exploring the foundations of climate action. The location is currently listed as to be determined . Experiential Learning Trip — May 2027 Participants will take part in an experiential learning trip designed to connect the cohort s learning with real-world climate contexts. The destination is also currently listed as to be determined . Concordia Summit and Graduation — September 2027 The programme concludes in New York City , where participants will attend the 2027 Concordia Annual Summit , reflect on their development, graduate from the Climate Cohort, and become part of a broader global leadership community. Strategic Workshops Participants will take part in expert-led workshops that provide both theoretical and practical learning. These workshops are designed to: Deepen participants understanding of climate systems Challenge existing assumptions Introduce practical tools Develop analytical skills Connect climate concepts with real-world work Help participants apply learning directly to their initiatives The workshops will be connected to the programme s three thematic pillars. Personalized Capacity-Building A major component of the programme is individualized support. Participants will receive capacity-building tailored to the needs of the cohort and their work. Areas may include: Strategy Governance Communications Partnership building Leadership Organizational development This means participants will not only learn together as a group but will also have opportunities to strengthen skills relevant to their individual leadership and organizational challenges. Cohort Reflection Circles The Climate Cohort also includes Cohort Reflection Circles . These sessions provide participants with a space to: Share experiences Discuss challenges Exchange ideas Reflect on their work Learn from other participants Explore possible strategies together Build relationships with fellow climate leaders The emphasis is on peer-to-peer learning and honest exchange rather than only formal instruction. RGL Engagement Circles Participants will also have the opportunity to share their knowledge with younger members of the broader Rising Global Leaders community. Through RGL Engagement Circles , Climate Cohort participants, referred to as Changemakers, can lead discussions and workshops for individuals who are at earlier stages of their leadership journeys. This creates an additional opportunity for participants to reflect on their own experiences and contribute to the development of younger emerging leaders. Mentorship, Networking and Global Exposure The Climate Cohort is designed not only as an educational programme but also as a leadership network. The programme provides opportunities for: Mentorship Peer exchange International networking Experiential learning Engagement with other social-impact leaders Connections across different climate initiatives and communities Libra Philanthropies describes Rising Global Leaders as a broader programme intended to connect emerging leaders through mentorship, immersive experiences, and peer-to-peer exchange. The Climate Cohort therefore provides participants with the opportunity to develop relationships beyond their immediate organizations and communities. Programme Time Commitment Participants should expect approximately 100–110 hours of active participation throughout the nine-month programme. This includes: In-person workshops Virtual sessions Reflection circles Independent activities Additional engagements The most intensive periods are expected to coincide with the three in-person gatherings: February: Kickoff, approximately four days May: Experiential/Immersion Trip, approximately four days September: New York City trip and Concordia Summit, approximately three days Participants are expected to attend scheduled sessions in order to fully participate in the programme. Is the Climate Cohort Fully Funded? Yes. According to the official Libra Philanthropies programme page, all travel and programme-related costs will be fully covered by Libra Philanthropies . This is particularly relevant because the programme includes international or multi-location in-person components, including the experiential learning trip and the final New York City gathering. The programme information does not state a separate personal stipend or salary for participants, so applicants should distinguish between covered programme/travel costs and a personal financial award. Apply HERE How Many Participants Will Be Selected? The 2027 Climate Cohort is expected to include 6–8 participants . The small cohort is intended to allow participants to develop deeper relationships, collaborate closely, and receive more tailored support throughout the programme. This makes the application process selective, particularly because the programme is intended for leaders who are already engaged in climate-focused work. Application Process The application process consists of several stages. Step 1: Complete the Online Application Applicants must complete the written application, which takes approximately 30 minutes according to the official programme page. Applicants must also submit a short recorded video introducing themselves and their climate-related work . Step 2: Application Review Libra Philanthropies will review submitted applications against the programme s eligibility and selection criteria. The organization uses a rolling review process as applications are received. Step 3: Interviews Shortlisted candidates will be invited to an interview with members of the programme team. Step 4: Final Selection Selected participants will be notified before the 2027 Climate Cohort is publicly announced. The official timeline lists: Applications open: September 22, 2026 Applications close: October 23, 2026 Rolling application review Shortlisted interviews: November 2026 Final cohort announcement: December 2026 Important Deadline The application deadline for the 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort is: October 23, 2026. Applicants should complete the written application and recorded video submission before the deadline. What Kind of Climate Work Is Relevant? The programme does not limit applicants to one specific climate discipline. The official eligibility language focuses on climate-focused initiatives or organizations and community-grounded climate work. This can potentially include initiatives working around areas such as: Climate adaptation Community resilience Environmental sustainability Climate policy Climate education Energy Land and natural resources Community development Climate finance Environmental justice Locally led climate solutions However, applicants should ensure that their actual initiative demonstrates a clear connection to climate change and is grounded in the needs and experiences of the communities they serve. What Makes This Opportunity Different? The Climate Cohort is structured around the idea that climate leadership requires more than technical knowledge about climate change. Participants are expected to develop an understanding of the systems surrounding climate action . This includes understanding: Who makes climate decisions How climate priorities are established How funding influences climate solutions How institutions shape action How communities respond to climate impacts How leaders can build influence How organizations can strengthen their strategies How different leaders can collaborate across communities and borders The programme therefore combines leadership development, organizational capacity-building, experiential learning and climate-focused systems thinking . Learn more HERE Why Community-Grounded Leadership Matters A defining feature of the Climate Cohort is its focus on leaders whose climate work is connected to communities. Rather than focusing exclusively on large institutions or established organizations, the programme seeks leaders who are already working within or alongside communities to address climate-related challenges. This reflects the broader philosophy of Libra Philanthropies Rising Global Leaders programme, which describes Changemakers as community-based leaders who understand local challenges firsthand and are already taking action, often with limited resources. About Libra Philanthropies Libra Philanthropies was established in 2023 by the Logothetis family as an independent 501(c)(3) foundation. Its work focuses on developing partnerships, creating programmes, supporting changemakers, and addressing social needs internationally. The organization describes its broader Rising Global Leaders programme as a platform for supporting emerging leaders at different stages of their leadership journeys. The programme has two broad participant pathways: Emerging Leaders , supporting individuals at earlier stages of leadership Changemakers , supporting community-based leaders who are already creating impact The 2027 Climate Cohort falls within the Changemakers pathway. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants can strengthen their preparation by making sure their application clearly communicates the connection between their leadership, their initiative, their community, and climate action . 1. Clearly explain your climate initiative Do not simply state that you care about climate change. Explain what your initiative actually does. 2. Demonstrate your leadership role The programme is designed for people already leading or playing a significant role in climate-focused work. Explain your responsibilities and contribution. 3. Show your community connection The initiative should be grounded in the needs and experiences of the communities it serves. Explain how you understand those needs and how the community is connected to your work. 4. Explain what you want to learn Think about the leadership, organizational, strategic, governance, communications, or partnership skills that would help you strengthen your work. 5. Prepare your video carefully The recorded video is part of the application. Use it as an opportunity to communicate who you are, what you work on, and why the Climate Cohort is relevant to your leadership journey. 6. Demonstrate willingness to collaborate The programme includes peer learning, reflection circles and shared engagements, so applicants should be prepared to learn from and contribute to a cohort of other leaders. Conclusion The 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort by Libra Philanthropies is a nine-month leadership development and experiential learning programme for emerging climate leaders aged 20–35 who are already working through climate-focused initiatives or organizations. The programme combines strategic workshops, personalized capacity-building, peer reflection, mentorship and networking, experiential learning, in-person convenings and opportunities to engage with younger emerging leaders . Participants will also attend an experiential learning trip and conclude the programme at the 2027 Concordia Annual Summit in New York City. The programme is designed around three central themes: understanding the climate system; local adaptation and community resilience; and moving from participation to climate action and influence . The cohort will consist of approximately 6–8 participants , and all programme-related and travel costs are covered by Libra Philanthropies. Applications opened on September 22, 2026 , and close on October 23, 2026 . Applicants should be between 20 and 35, already leading or significantly contributing to a climate-focused initiative or organization, and working on climate action that is grounded in community needs and experiences. for more opportunities click HERE The post Libra Philanthropies 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort: 9-Month Leadership Programme for Emerging Climate Leaders appeared first on Opportunities for Youth .

title: Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027: Up to $10,000 in Project Funding and Leadership Support for Community Health Equity Leaders
summary: The Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 is now accepting applications from community leaders with ideas for projects that can advance health equity and address social determinants of health within the M Health Fairview service area. The year-long fellowship is designed to help participants strengthen their leadership, develop their project ideas, receive expert guidance, and turn community-focused ideas into practical action. The program, offered through the M Health Fairview Center for Community Health Equity , combines leadership development, education, coaching, technical assistance, peer learning, networking, and financial support. Each selected fellow can receive up to $10,000 in project funding , in addition to a $3,000 participation stipend intended to help support costs associated with participating in the fellowship. For the 2027 cohort, eight fellows will be selected. The fellowship will run from January through December 2027 , with sessions delivered through a combination of in-person meetings across the seven-county metro area and virtual sessions. What Is the Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship? The Accelerator Fellowship is a 12-month leadership development program created to support community leaders who are working on innovative approaches to health equity and the social conditions that influence people s health and wellbeing. Rather than requiring applicants to already have a completely developed project, the fellowship provides space for participants to develop, test, refine, and implement their ideas during the fellowship year. The program is particularly focused on helping community leaders move from an identified community challenge toward a practical project with achievable goals and measurable activities. According to M Health Fairview, fellows receive structured support to: Build and strengthen leadership capacity Sharpen their vision for community change Develop and refine a health equity project Receive coaching and technical assistance Learn about health equity and project implementation Connect with other community leaders Develop partnerships and community relationships Put their project ideas into action Receive financial resources to support project implementation Each fellow will be part of a cohort of eight community leaders who learn and grow together throughout the year. Up to $10,000 in Project Funding One of the major components of the 2027 Accelerator Fellowship is financial support for fellows community projects. Each fellow can receive up to $10,000 in project funding to help bring their health equity project to life. Importantly, applicants do not need to have a fully developed project when they apply. The fellowship provides the full year for fellows to build, test, and refine their approaches with support from coaches, experts, and peers. The application specifically asks applicants to explain how the project funding will support their proposed activities and requires a draft project budget outlining expected expenses of up to $10,000. In addition to project funding, the official FAQ states that fellows receive a $3,000 stipend to support participation in the fellowship. This may help cover costs such as compensation for time, transportation, childcare, or other incidental expenses. ( mhealthfairview.org ) What Does the Fellowship Provide? The Accelerator Fellowship offers several forms of support throughout the year. 1. Health Equity Education Fellows participate in an educational curriculum covering health equity, program development, implementation, and related areas of community work. The curriculum is designed to give participants both conceptual knowledge and practical tools that they can apply to their projects. 2. Coaching and Technical Assistance Participants receive coaching and technical assistance from experts working in relevant fields. This allows fellows to receive guidance while developing their projects, addressing challenges, refining their approaches, and moving from ideas toward implementation. 3. Project Funding Fellows receive up to $10,000 to support implementation of their health equity projects. This funding is intended to help participants turn their ideas into practical community initiatives rather than simply developing theoretical proposals. 4. Networking and Peer Learning The fellowship creates opportunities for participants to build relationships with other community leaders and professionals whose interests align with their work. Because the eight fellows progress through the program together, the cohort provides an environment for shared learning, collaboration, and exchange of different perspectives. What Types of Projects Can Applicants Propose? The fellowship is focused on projects that address health equity or social determinants of health within the eligible service area. A project does not necessarily need to be a traditional healthcare project. Health equity can involve the broader conditions that influence people s ability to live healthy lives, including issues involving housing, food, education, community connection, environment, access to resources, and other structural or social factors. The 2026 cohort illustrates the breadth of projects that can fit within the program. Previous fellows worked on initiatives involving culturally responsive nutrition, community barbering and mentorship, rural wellness, housing stability, Indigenous food and knowledge systems, transitional housing and recovery, and grief and trauma education. This demonstrates that applicants can approach health equity from different professional, cultural, community, and disciplinary perspectives. What Makes a Strong Project Idea? According to the fellowship s published criteria, a strong project should be community-rooted , meaning that it responds to a real and identified need within a specific community and demonstrates community engagement in shaping the idea. The project should also be equity-focused , with the goal of reducing health disparities or addressing structural barriers to equity. Applicants should also demonstrate that their project is: Realistic Actionable Appropriately scoped for the fellowship period Supported by achievable objectives Based on a reasonable budget Connected to an identified community need The program also states that it values diversity of perspective over formal titles , meaning applicants are not required to rely solely on conventional professional credentials to demonstrate their ability to contribute. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Who Is the Fellowship Looking For? The Accelerator Fellowship is designed for community leaders , and applicants can come from different professional backgrounds and career stages. The published FAQ states that applicants from all backgrounds, professions, and career stages are welcome. The fellowship looks for individuals who have contributed to their communities professionally or personally and who demonstrate commitment to health equity. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Applicants are expected to demonstrate qualities such as: Community orientation Commitment to health equity Collaboration Resourcefulness Commitment to participating fully Authenticity Openness and curiosity A solution-oriented approach The fellowship is specifically for individual applicants rather than organizations . ( mhealthfairview.org ) Eligibility Requirements for the 2027 Cohort Applicants must meet the following requirements: Have a project idea focused on advancing health equity in their community. Plan to implement the project within Fairview s service area. Be at least 18 years old. Not currently be employed by Fairview Health Services. Have related experience, relationships, or community ties to the issue or topic they want to address. Be available to attend all required fellowship sessions. The program is therefore not simply looking for people with an interesting idea. Applicants should be able to demonstrate some meaningful relationship with the issue or community they want to serve. Where Must the Project Be Implemented? A particularly important eligibility requirement is geography. The project must be implemented within the M Health Fairview service area . The published eligible counties are: Minnesota Anoka Benton Carver Chisago Dakota Hennepin Isanti Itasca Kanabec Mille Lacs Pine Ramsey Saint Louis Scott Sherburne Washington Wright Wisconsin Pierce County Saint Croix County Therefore, this is not an open worldwide fellowship . The proposed project must be located within the specified M Health Fairview service-area geography. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Fellowship Duration and Format The 2027 Accelerator Fellowship runs for 12 months, from January through December 2027 . Sessions will combine: In-person sessions Virtual sessions Workshops Learning activities Leadership development Project work Coaching Peer learning Most months will include two sessions, which may consist of full-day in-person meetings or shorter virtual sessions. The published FAQ estimates approximately 105 hours of in-class time over the fellowship, in addition to the time fellows need to spend implementing their individual projects. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Areas Covered by the Fellowship Curriculum The program s curriculum is designed to develop both leadership and practical project-management capabilities. Topics include: Orientation and foundations Funding and evaluation Project planning Project management Strategic communications Community engagement Community mapping and collaboration Public health, policy, environment and systems change Leadership and partnerships Learning and coaching Reflection and sharing Celebration and showcase The curriculum can adapt to the needs of the cohort, and the organizers note that session topics may change. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Application Requirements Applicants should prepare several components before submitting the application. The required materials include: Basic personal information Two letters of recommendation Narrative responses to the application questions Additional information about the proposed project A draft project budget If the proposed project is affiliated with an organization, at least one recommendation/support letter should come from that organization. Applicants should also download and review the full application and budget template before completing the online application. The application process involves: Reviewing the full application form. Reviewing and completing the draft budget template. Completing the online application. Uploading two recommendation/support letters. Uploading the draft budget. Submitting the complete application before the deadline. Application Questions The application asks applicants to explain both their health equity vision and their leadership journey . Your Vision for Health Equity Applicants are asked to explain: What health equity challenge they want to address Why the issue matters to their community What has contributed to their understanding of the issue Why they are personally positioned to address it What transformation they hope to achieve What impact they intend to make What their proposed project involves How the $10,000 project funding would support the work Their three primary objectives for the fellowship period The application places a 1,500-character limit on the problem, proposal, and objectives responses. Your Leadership Journey Applicants are also asked to discuss their leadership experience and how their background, identity, relationships, and life experiences have shaped their approach to leadership. The application allows applicants to provide examples of formal or informal leadership and explain how their leadership journey connects to their proposed project. This section has a 2,000-character limit or a three-minute video option , with applicants choosing one format. Applicants are additionally asked how the fellowship could support their leadership development, what they could contribute to the cohort, why the timing is appropriate, and what skills, resources, or technical assistance would help them achieve their health equity vision. Selection and Number of Fellows The 2027 fellowship will select eight applicants . The selection process is competitive. Semi-finalists are expected to be notified in late October and invited to participate in an interview in early November. The interview can be conducted virtually if needed. Final cohort selections are expected to be announced in mid-November, with all applicants notified of final decisions by late November. Important Application Deadline The deadline for the Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 is: Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. CST. Applicants should ensure that the complete application, required recommendation letters, and draft budget are submitted before the deadline. Is This a Scholarship or a Grant? The Accelerator Fellowship is structured primarily as a leadership development fellowship with project funding , rather than a traditional academic scholarship. The program combines: Leadership development Health equity education Coaching Technical assistance Peer networking Project implementation support Up to $10,000 in project funding A $3,000 participation stipend It is also not a degree or credit-bearing academic program. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Why This Fellowship May Be Relevant to Community Leaders The fellowship is designed around the idea that many health challenges cannot be addressed through healthcare services alone. Community conditions, social environments, access to resources, housing, food, education, relationships, and other factors can influence health outcomes. M Health Fairview s Center for Community Health Equity works with community partners to address these broader determinants and reduce disparities. ( mhealthfairview.org ) The Accelerator Fellowship therefore provides a structured environment in which community leaders can develop projects that respond to issues they understand through direct community experience. The combination of project funding and leadership development also allows fellows to work on both sides of the challenge: strengthening their own capacity as leaders while developing a practical response to a community health equity issue. Tips for Preparing a Strong Application Applicants should pay close attention to the relationship between their community, problem, project, leadership experience, and proposed outcomes . A strong application should clearly explain: 1. The community problem Identify a specific health equity challenge rather than describing a broad social issue without context. 2. Why the problem matters Explain how the issue affects the community and why addressing it is important. 3. Your connection to the issue The fellowship specifically asks applicants to demonstrate related experience, relationships, or community ties. 4. Your proposed solution Explain what you want to do and how the project would address the identified problem. 5. Your objectives Define three realistic objectives that can be pursued between January and December 2027. 6. Your use of funding Show how the proposed $10,000 would directly support project activities. 7. Your leadership story The application is interested not only in the project but also in the person leading it. Explain how your experiences have shaped your approach to leadership. 8. Your readiness Because fellows are expected to participate throughout the year, applicants should demonstrate that they can commit to the program s sessions and project implementation requirements. Learn more HERE Conclusion The Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 provides a year-long opportunity for community leaders to develop health equity projects while strengthening their leadership skills and community connections. The program combines education, coaching, technical assistance, networking, and financial support, with each fellow eligible for up to $10,000 in project funding and a $3,000 participation stipend . ( mhealthfairview.org ) The fellowship is particularly focused on individuals who understand a community health equity challenge through their experience, relationships, or community ties and who have an idea they want to develop into practical action. Eight fellows will be selected for the 2027 cohort, which will run from January through December 2027. Applicants should carefully review the geographic requirements because projects must be implemented within the specified M Health Fairview service area. The application deadline is October 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. CST . Who Can Apply? Category of qualifying people: Individual community leaders aged 18 or older with a health equity project idea and a meaningful connection to the issue or community they intend to serve. Key qualifications Applicants must: Be at least 18 years old. Have a project idea focused on advancing health equity. Have related experience, relationships, or community ties to the issue. Plan to implement the project within the eligible M Health Fairview service area. Be available to participate in all required fellowship sessions. Not currently be employed by Fairview Health Services. Apply as an individual rather than as an organization. Applicants may come from different professions, backgrounds, and career stages ; the program states that diversity of perspective is valued over formal titles. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Apply for the 2027 Accelerator Fellowship View the official M Health Fairview fellowship information MORE OPPORTUNITIES HERE The post Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027: Up to $10,000 in Project Funding and Leadership Support for Community Health Equity Leaders appeared first on Opportunities for Youth .

title: Education Endowment Foundation Research Funding Opportunities: Three Calls for Research Proposals in England’s Education Sector
summary: The Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) has announced three research opportunities inviting legally constituted organisations and research teams to submit proposals examining important issues in education across England. The calls focus on inclusive mainstream education and Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), technical and vocational teaching for learners aged 16–19, and the continuity of exam boards for GCSE resit learners. These opportunities are particularly relevant to education research organisations, universities, research consultancies, policy institutes, and research consortia with expertise in qualitative research, education, pedagogy, impact evaluation, process evaluation, and the 16–19 education sector. The three calls seek to generate evidence that can contribute to future EEF guidance, research commissioning, and education policy. Depending on the opportunity, successful research teams may be expected to conduct school or college visits, classroom observations, quantitative analysis, qualitative research, feasibility work, or evaluation activities. Below is a detailed overview of all three EEF research opportunities, including their objectives, research questions, methodological expectations, eligibility requirements, and application deadlines. 1. Practice Review on the Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies The Education Endowment Foundation is commissioning a practice review examining how schools in England are developing inclusion strategies and approaching their use of the Inclusive Mainstream Fund (IMF). The research comes at a time of significant policy development around creating a more inclusive mainstream education system in England, particularly for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities. Background and Context The Government’s 2026 Schools White Paper set out an ambition to create a more inclusive mainstream education system in which schools are appropriately equipped and funded to support children with SEND to achieve and thrive within inclusive mainstream settings. As part of this broader reform agenda, the Department for Education has committed to a package of measures intended to strengthen inclusion within mainstream schools. One of these measures is the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. In addition, the Department for Education expects all state-maintained mainstream schools to develop and publish an inclusion strategy on their websites by 31 December each year. These developments create an opportunity to understand how schools are responding to the new expectations in practice. The EEF therefore wants to build an evidence base around how schools are developing their inclusion strategies and making decisions concerning the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. What the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Will Examine The practice review aims to develop a clearer picture of current practice across different school settings. In particular, the research will: Map current approaches to developing inclusion strategies across school settings. Examine how schools are approaching spending through the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. Explore differences in practice between schools and settings. Investigate reported changes in behaviours and beliefs associated with the introduction of the new policies. Explore changes in decision-making that may be connected to the new inclusion policies. Identify emerging approaches that may be relevant to future EEF guidance and research. The research is therefore not simply focused on whether schools have developed inclusion strategies. It is also concerned with understanding the processes behind those strategies and how schools are making decisions about resources and inclusion. How the Research Findings Will Be Used The findings from this research are expected to have several applications within education policy, research and practice. The evidence may inform future development of EEF guidance relating to inclusion, including resources such as the EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching. The findings may also contribute to: Future EEF research activity. The development of additional evidence-based resources. Understanding of emerging practices in mainstream schools. Advice provided to policymakers. Future research priorities concerning inclusive education and SEND. The main output from the project will be a written research report. The report is expected to be published by the end of March 2027. Research Approach The EEF welcomes proposals capable of addressing both the primary and secondary research questions. Applicants are encouraged to consider a variety of research methods and may propose innovative approaches where appropriate. A mixed-methods approach may be suitable for the project, depending on the proposed research questions and methodology. Applicants should therefore demonstrate clearly how their proposed methodology will allow them to develop a meaningful understanding of: How schools are developing inclusion strategies. How schools are approaching Inclusive Mainstream Fund spending. Whether behaviours and beliefs are changing. How decision-making may be changing in response to the policies. How practices vary between different school settings. Who Can Apply for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Practice Review? The opportunity is primarily relevant to organisations and research teams with expertise in education research, particularly research involving schools, inclusion, SEND, policy implementation, and qualitative or mixed-methods research. Potential applicants may include: Universities and higher education institutions. Education research organisations. Research consultancies. Policy research organisations. Specialist education research teams. Consortia bringing together complementary research expertise. Applicants should carefully review the complete EEF invitation to tender and selection criteria before submitting a proposal. Deadline for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Opportunity Completed applications must be submitted through the designated Form Assembly application form by: 12pm on Monday, 19 October 2026. Applicants should allow sufficient time to review the tender documentation, prepare their methodology and supporting information, and complete the online submission before the deadline. APPLY HERE 2. Practice Review on 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching The second EEF research opportunity focuses on teaching practices within technical and vocational education for learners aged 16–19. The research will investigate current teaching approaches across technical and vocational subject areas and examine how these practices relate to the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework (ITTECF) used in schools. The project is intended to provide a clearer understanding of what teaching currently looks like in technical and vocational settings. Project Summary The practice review will involve detailed observations of teaching practice across a selection of technical and vocational subject areas in the 16–19 sector. Researchers will examine teaching in classrooms and workshops to build a picture of current practice. The research is expected to contribute to understanding: The teaching approaches currently being used. How frequently particular teaching practices are observed. Whether practices identified in the schools ITTECF are also used in technical and vocational education. Whether technical and vocational teachers use other teaching approaches that are not represented in the ITTECF. Whether there are common patterns among colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas. The findings may subsequently inform future EEF research commissioning and guidance for the technical and vocational education sector. Main Research Aims The project has several interconnected aims. 1. Understand Current Teaching Practice The research will examine teaching practices currently being used in technical and vocational education settings. This is intended to provide a practical snapshot of teaching across relevant 16–19 settings. 2. Examine Use of ITTECF Teaching Practices Researchers will investigate whether teaching practices identified within the schools Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework are being used in technical and vocational education. The research will also consider whether some of these practices are more prevalent than others. 3. Identify Additional Teaching Practices The project will look beyond the practices contained in the ITTECF. Researchers will identify whether there are other teaching practices commonly observed in technical and vocational education that are not included within the ITTECF framework. 4. Explore High-Performing Colleges The research will also examine whether colleges performing particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas demonstrate common approaches to teaching. This could include investigating whether successful colleges use particular combinations or amounts of the identified teaching practices. Main Research Question The central research question is: Do vocational and technical teachers use the teaching practices identified from the schools ITTECF in their day-to-day teaching? This question will provide the foundation for the practice review. Secondary Research Questions The research will also investigate several related questions, including: Are some of the teaching practices more prevalent than others? Are other teaching practices observed that are not included in the ITTECF? Do colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas use different combinations of the teaching practices? Do these high-performing colleges use different amounts of particular teaching practices? Answering these questions will help the EEF understand whether teaching approaches used in technical and vocational education closely resemble those used in schools or whether there are distinctive practices within the 16–19 sector. Methodological Expectations The project will involve primary research intended to provide a snapshot of current teaching practice in vocational and technical education for learners aged 16–19. The EEF is open to proposals using different research methodologies. Applicants are encouraged to propose approaches that can effectively answer the primary and secondary research questions. Innovative research approaches are also welcomed. However, college visits and observations are expected to be a key component of the research plan. This means applicants should carefully consider how their proposed methodology will allow researchers to observe teaching directly within technical and vocational settings. Feasibility Phase Proposals are expected to include a short feasibility phase. This feasibility phase should involve a small number of colleges and will help researchers test: The suitability of the subject areas identified for the research. The proposed list of classroom teaching practices. The practicality of the observation approach. Whether the proposed research design can generate useful data. Including a feasibility phase will allow the research team to refine its approach before implementing the broader practice review. Who Should Apply? The EEF is seeking research teams with: Experience conducting qualitative research in education. A strong understanding of the 16–19 education sector. Knowledge of pedagogy in England. Experience designing and implementing education research. The ability to conduct research within colleges and technical or vocational education settings. Applications can be submitted by either a single research team or a consortium. Consortia may be particularly appropriate where different organisations can contribute complementary expertise. However, a consortium must be able to demonstrate that its members can work effectively together and maintain the quality and efficiency of the research project. Organisations Eligible to Apply This opportunity is open to legally constituted organisations rather than individuals. Importantly, applicants do not have to be members of the EEF s existing panel of evaluators. The organisation also does not necessarily have to be based in England. International organisations may apply, provided they can demonstrate that: Their research outputs will be relevant to the English education system. The proposed research team has sufficient understanding of the English 16–19 education context. The proposal represents value for money. The organisation has the appropriate legal constitution to undertake the work. This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to eligible education research organisations outside England, provided they can demonstrate appropriate knowledge and contextual expertise. Deadline for the 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching Research Opportunity Interested applicants must submit their full research proposals by: 5pm on Friday, 16 October 2026. Questions relating to the tender and research proposals should be directed to the EEF contact provided in the original tender documentation. Research proposals should be sent to: post-16@eefoundation.org.uk 3. 16–19 Setting Choices: GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resits among learners aged 16–19 in England. The EEF is seeking research proposals to investigate whether maintaining the same exam board between a learner s original GCSE sitting and their subsequent GCSE resit is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes. This research forms part of the EEF s Setting Choices programme. Overview of the GCSE Resit Research The project will investigate whether sitting a GCSE resit with the same examination board used for the learner s initial GCSE sitting affects outcomes in English and mathematics. The research will compare continuity with changing exam boards. The central issue is whether maintaining the same examination board provides any measurable difference in outcomes for learners undertaking GCSE resits between the ages of 16 and 19. Background to the Research The research takes place against a wider concern about attainment differences during the 16–19 phase of education. According to the background information provided by the EEF, the socio-economic attainment gap is particularly significant during the 16–19 phase. The Education Policy Institute s 2026 annual report reported that the 16–19 disadvantage gap had remained broadly stable at approximately 3.3–3.4 grades, reaching 3.4 grades in 2025. The EEF describes the 16–19 phase as an important opportunity to improve attainment and strengthen young people s future life chances. Within this broader context, the EEF is interested in examining factors that could potentially influence the success of GCSE resit learners. Why Exam Board Continuity Is Being Studied The choice of examination board may influence aspects of a learner s resit experience. The EEF s research background notes that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools for English, mathematics, or both. Other colleges do not maintain this alignment. The rationale for continuity is that learners may benefit from familiarity with the examination structure and expectations associated with the same exam board. At the same time, changing examination boards could potentially offer a learner a different approach. The purpose of the proposed research is not to assume that one approach is beneficial, but to generate evidence about whether continuity is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes. Existing Evidence and Rationale The EEF s background information references the Education Policy Institute s Drivers of Success report, which identified examination board choice and continuity with a learner s original examination board as potentially relevant to GCSE resit success. The EEF has also surveyed its college network, consisting of approximately 90 colleges. The survey found that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools, while others do not use such alignment. This variation in practice provides an opportunity to investigate the issue through research. Main Research Question The central research question is: Does sitting a GCSE resit with the same exam board as the initial sitting, compared with using a different exam board, affect English and mathematics outcomes for 16–19 resit learners? The research is expected to provide evidence capable of assessing the relationship between examination board continuity and learner outcomes. Expected Research Design The EEF expects the research to include several important components. 1. Causal Impact Evaluation The project is expected to include a causal impact evaluation using a quasi-experimental design. This component is intended to investigate whether differences in exam board continuity are associated with differences in learner outcomes while addressing relevant methodological challenges. 2. Implementation and Process Evaluation A light-touch Implementation and Process Evaluation is also expected. This component can help researchers understand how exam board continuity operates in practice and provide context for interpreting the impact evaluation findings. 3. Subgroup Analysis The research is also expected to include subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners. This will allow researchers to investigate whether the relationship between exam board continuity and outcomes differs for learners experiencing disadvantage. Who Should Apply? The EEF is inviting research teams with experience conducting: Impact evaluations. Process evaluations. Education research. Research within the 16–19 sector. Quasi-experimental research. Quantitative analysis of learner outcomes. The EEF is interested in expressions of interest from individual research teams as well as consortia with complementary expertise. Consortia should demonstrate that their members can work effectively together to ensure the quality and efficiency of the research. Organisational Eligibility Applications are accepted from legally constituted organisations rather than individuals. Researchers do not need to be members of the EEF s panel of evaluators. Organisations based outside England are also eligible to apply. However, international organisations must demonstrate that their teams possess the knowledge and expertise necessary to undertake research relevant to the English education system and complete the proposed work effectively. Deadline for the GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity Opportunity Interested applicants must submit their Expression of Interest through the designated application form by: 5pm on Monday, 12 October 2026. Applicants should ensure that their EOI addresses the requirements specified in the EEF tender documentation and demonstrates the research team s relevant expertise. Comparison of the Three EEF Research Opportunities Although all three opportunities are focused on education research, they address different areas of the English education system. A strong proposal should be closely aligned with the research questions and methodological expectations of the relevant call. For example, applicants for the technical and vocational teaching review should demonstrate knowledge of qualitative education research, pedagogy and the 16–19 sector. Applicants for the GCSE resit project should demonstrate appropriate impact and process evaluation experience. Knowledge of the English Education System International applicants should pay particular attention to demonstrating their understanding of the English education system. The EEF explicitly indicates that organisations based outside England can apply, but they must demonstrate that their research will be relevant to England and that their teams have the necessary knowledge. Appropriate Methodology Proposals should directly address the research questions. Depending on the opportunity, applicants may need to demonstrate expertise in: Qualitative research. Quantitative research. Mixed-methods research. Classroom observation. College visits. Quasi-experimental designs. Impact evaluation. Implementation and process evaluation. Subgroup analysis. Feasibility studies. Collaboration and Consortia Organisations applying as a consortium should clearly establish how responsibilities will be divided and how the partners will work together. The EEF is interested in consortia that bring complementary expertise while maintaining efficient project management and research quality. Relevance and Value for Money Applicants should demonstrate how the proposed work will contribute useful evidence and represent value for money. This is particularly important for organisations applying from outside England. Who Qualifies for These EEF Opportunities? The opportunities are primarily intended for legally constituted organisations and research teams , rather than individual applicants. Relevant applicants may include: Universities and higher education institutions. Education research organisations. Research institutes. Policy research organisations. Research consultancies. Specialist education research organisations. Consortia combining complementary research expertise. For the Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies review, applicants should have relevant expertise in education research, inclusion, SEND, school practice, policy implementation, qualitative research, mixed-methods research, or related areas. For the 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching review, applicants should have experience conducting qualitative education research and a strong understanding of the 16–19 sector and pedagogy in England. For the GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity evaluation, applicants should have experience conducting impact and process evaluations, particularly within the 16–19 education sector. Visit HERE to learn more about the Education Endowment Foundation Research Funding Opportunities. Countries and Regions The calls are focused on the education system in England , but organisations do not necessarily have to be physically based in England. The EEF states that organisations based outside England may apply for the relevant opportunities, provided they can demonstrate the knowledge and expertise required to conduct research relevant to the English education system. Accordingly, eligible organisations may potentially apply from England, elsewhere in the United Kingdom, or other countries , subject to the specific requirements of the applicable tender and the organisation s ability to demonstrate relevant expertise and value for money. These are institutional research opportunities rather than individual scholarships, fellowships or internships , so applicants should apply through an eligible organisation rather than as an individual researcher. Conclusion The Education Endowment Foundation s three new research opportunities provide organisations with the opportunity to contribute evidence to important questions affecting education in England. The first opportunity focuses on inclusive mainstream education , examining how schools are developing inclusion strategies and approaching the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. The research is intended to strengthen understanding of current practice and inform future guidance, research and policy. The second opportunity examines technical and vocational teaching among learners aged 16–19 . Researchers will observe teaching practice across selected subject areas and investigate how teaching approaches in technical and vocational settings compare with practices identified in the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework. The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resit exam board continuity , investigating whether maintaining the same examination board between a learner s initial GCSE sitting and their resit affects English and mathematics outcomes. The project is expected to use a quasi-experimental impact evaluation alongside a light-touch implementation and process evaluation and subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners. For organisations with relevant research expertise, these calls offer opportunities to undertake research with potential relevance to education practice, evidence-based guidance and policymaking in England. Applicants should carefully review the full tender requirements, ensure that their proposed methodology directly addresses the relevant research questions, and submit their applications before the applicable deadline. title: Next-Geo Program 2027: Pan-European Research and Training Fellowship in Geoeconomics for PhD Students and Early Postdocs
summary: The Next-Geo Program 2027 is inviting applications from advanced PhD students and early Postdoctoral researchers working in economics and closely related quantitative fields who are conducting research on geoeconomics . Now entering its second year, Next-Geo is a one-year pan-European research and training programme designed to support the next generation of researchers working at the intersection of economics and geopolitics. The programme is coordinated by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in cooperation with CEPR, Bocconi University through the Institute for European Policymaking, and the Oxford University Department of Economics , with funding from Stiftung Mercator . Each year, the programme brings together a carefully selected cohort of approximately 10 junior scholars to develop their research expertise, strengthen their professional networks and advance a research or policy project in geoeconomics. Applications submitted by October 31, 2026 are guaranteed full consideration for the 2027 cohort. The organisers aim to finalise the selection of successful candidates by the end of November 2026 . About the Next-Geo Program 2027 The Next-Geo Program is a specialised research and training programme focusing exclusively on the growing field of geoeconomics . The programme responds to the increasing importance of the relationship between economic policy and geopolitics in a rapidly changing global environment. While demand for researchers and policy experts with expertise in geoeconomics is growing, the programme notes that systematic training specifically focused on the field remains limited. Next-Geo was established to help address this gap by providing advanced research training, mentoring, policy-oriented development and networking opportunities for promising early-career researchers. The programme is intended to complement, rather than replace, the doctoral or postdoctoral training participants receive at their home universities or research institutions. It provides a dedicated environment where researchers can focus specifically on geoeconomic questions while remaining enrolled or employed at their existing European institution. What Is Geoeconomics? Geoeconomics broadly examines the relationship between economic activity, economic policy and geopolitical power . The Next-Geo programme recognises that economic and geopolitical developments are increasingly interconnected. Issues such as international trade, economic security, sanctions, industrial policy, energy transitions and global financial flows can have implications that extend beyond traditional economic analysis. The programme therefore welcomes research addressing a broad range of geoeconomic topics. Potential research areas include: Economic security Trade coercion Trade fragmentation Industrial policy Sanctions design Sanctions evasion Global financial flows Economic aid Climate transition Energy transition Defence economics The list is not presented as an exhaustive set of research topics, meaning applicants working on other questions that fit within the broader field of geoeconomics may also be relevant to the programme. Purpose of the Next-Geo Program The programme has two closely connected objectives: research development and community building . Supporting the Next Generation of Geoeconomists Next-Geo aims to support highly promising PhD students and early Postdoctoral researchers whose work focuses on geoeconomics. The programme recognises that young researchers working in this area can be geographically dispersed across Europe and may sometimes be isolated within departments or academic communities that do not have specialised expertise in geoeconomics. By bringing these researchers together, Next-Geo seeks to create a stronger network connecting early-career scholars with each other and with leading senior researchers across institutions and countries. A One-Year Add-On Fellowship Programme Next-Geo has a one-year duration and is structured as an add-on fellowship programme . This distinction is important. The programme is designed to complement participants existing PhD or Postdoctoral work rather than replacing their home institution. Participants remain enrolled or employed at their existing university or research institution throughout the programme. Next-Geo does not provide a formal degree and does not create an employment relationship with the Kiel Institute. The programme therefore provides an additional research and training environment specifically focused on geoeconomics. What Does the Next-Geo Program Offer? Selected participants become part of a competitive cohort of junior researchers and receive research training, mentoring, networking opportunities and practical research support. The programme combines online and in-person activities throughout the academic year. Key elements include: 1. Advanced Coursework and Research Training Participants receive lectures and training covering research at the frontier of geoeconomics. The teaching is delivered by: Internationally renowned external scholars Researchers at the Kiel Institute Leading experts working in the field The objective is to expose participants to current research and strengthen their understanding of advanced questions in geoeconomics. 2. Research Feedback and Senior Mentoring Participants develop their own research or policy project during the programme. They receive feedback and mentoring from senior researchers and leading experts in geoeconomics. This provides participants with an opportunity to refine their projects, strengthen their research design and receive input from experienced scholars working in the field. 3. Research Assistant Support Promising research projects may receive support from a pool of four Next-Geo student research assistants . These research assistants are specifically hired at the Kiel Institute to support Next-Geo junior researchers. Support can be provided: In person at the Berlin office Remotely Or through a combination of these arrangements This research assistance can provide additional capacity for participants developing substantial research projects. 4. Funding for Data and AI Subscriptions Promising projects may also receive funding for research-related resources. This can include: Data purchases Subscriptions to frontier large language models and AI tools The programme specifically gives Claude and OpenAI as examples of AI services that may be supported. This component is intended to provide researchers with practical resources that can contribute to the development of their projects. 5. Travel and Accommodation Support The programme provides support for travel and accommodation expenses associated with in-person modules . On-site participation is expected, so this support is an important part of the programme s structure. Participants can therefore take part in the programme s physical workshops and modules without being expected to independently cover the stated travel and accommodation costs associated with those activities. Engagement With the Kiel Institute Participants also have the opportunity to become familiar with the work and activities of the Kiel Institute, which the programme describes as one of the leading institutions working on geoeconomics. The institute s activities and initiatives include: The annual Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics The LSE-Kiel-CEPR Conference on Defence Economics The Kiel Institute-led CEPR Research Policy Network on Geoeconomics and Security The Ukraine Support Tracker The Kiel Research Center on Geoeconomics This provides participants with opportunities to engage with research networks and initiatives connected to geoeconomics and related policy questions. Research and Policy Project Outcomes A central objective of the programme is for participants to complete a substantial research or policy project in geoeconomics . By the end of the programme, participants are expected to have developed a high-quality project. The strongest projects may have opportunities to be: Published as Kiel Institute working papers Published as CEPR working papers Developed into policy briefs Presented at conferences Presented at workshops Participants also receive a certificate of programme participation . The programme therefore places emphasis not only on training but also on producing a tangible research or policy output. Opportunities to Engage With Policymakers and Practitioners Next-Geo also connects researchers with people working outside traditional academic environments. Participants can engage with: Policymakers Think tanks Practitioners Academic researchers Policy experts These interactions take place through events and workshops at the Kiel-CEPR Research Hub in Berlin and at partner institutions. This policy-facing element is particularly relevant for researchers interested in producing work that can contribute to public-policy discussions in addition to academic debates. Programme Structure and Timeline The Next-Geo programme runs across one academic year and combines virtual learning with several in-person modules. The programme begins with an online kick-off during winter and progresses through research training, workshops and networking activities before concluding with the Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics in autumn. Winter: Online Kick-Off The programme begins with an online meeting in winter. During this stage, participants: Meet the other members of the cohort Present their research or policy project ideas Receive an introductory lecture Learn about the foundations of geoeconomics This initial stage establishes the basis for collaborative learning and project development. Spring: Lecture and Research Training The spring stage is titled “Best of Geoeconomics @ Kiel Institute.” This is a multi-day in-person module held in Kiel and/or Berlin . Activities include: Advanced academic lectures Lectures delivered by leading scholars Training in producing high-quality policy-relevant research Structured feedback on participants research projects This stage is designed to deepen participants academic understanding and help them improve their research designs and methodologies. Summer: Research and Policy Workshop The summer stage consists of a hands-on, multi-day Research and Policy Workshop . The workshop takes place in Berlin and/or another European location . Activities include: Presenting ongoing research projects Receiving feedback Interacting with policymakers Engaging with think tanks Connecting with practitioners Developing research communication skills Developing policy engagement skills Strengthening public outreach abilities The workshop is therefore intended to help researchers think beyond the academic paper and develop the skills needed to communicate research to policy and public audiences. Autumn: Geoeconomics Conference and Networking The programme concludes in autumn with the Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics in Berlin . Participants will: Attend the leading academic conference in the field Potentially present their research projects to an international expert audience Compete with peers for the best research paper or best policy brief Network with scholars Engage with political decision-makers The opportunity to potentially present research at the conference provides a further platform for participants to communicate their work to an international audience. European Institutional Affiliation Requirement The programme is designed for researchers conducting their PhD or Postdoctoral work at a European institution . Applicants must therefore generally be enrolled or employed at a European university or research institution. The call also states that European nationals at overseas institutions may be eligible in selected cases . This distinction is important because nationality and institutional affiliation are treated differently in the eligibility requirements. What the Next-Geo Programme Does Not Provide Applicants should understand the distinction between research support and personal financial support. The programme does not provide : An employment contract A stipend A living-expense allowance A formal degree Instead, it provides funding for: Travel for on-site modules Accommodation for on-site modules Research support Research assistant access Data purchases and/or AI subscriptions for promising projects Participants remain fully enrolled or employed at their home institution and do not receive employment or enrollment status at the Kiel Institute. This means that applicants should not regard Next-Geo as a replacement for their existing PhD funding or Postdoctoral employment. Application Requirements Applicants must submit their applications through the designated application form. Applications submitted by October 31, 2026 are guaranteed full consideration. The application must include the following materials: 1. Curriculum Vitae Applicants must submit a CV demonstrating their academic and research background. Given the programme s emphasis on an excellent track record, applicants should ensure that their CV clearly presents their research experience, publications where applicable, academic achievements and other relevant accomplishments. 2. Cover Letter A cover letter is required as part of the application. The letter should help explain the applicant s motivation for joining the programme and demonstrate the relationship between their research and Next-Geo s focus on geoeconomics. 3. One-Page Research Project Sketch Applicants must submit a one-page research project sketch . This document should present the proposed research or policy project that they intend to develop during the programme. Because the programme focuses specifically on geoeconomics, applicants should clearly demonstrate how their project fits within the field. Potential topics can include areas such as economic security, trade, sanctions, industrial policy, financial flows, energy, climate transition and defence economics. 4. Writing Sample Applicants must provide a writing sample. Examples identified by the programme include: A third-year paper A job market paper The writing sample provides an opportunity for applicants to demonstrate the quality of their academic research and writing. 5. Two Potential References Applicants must provide the names of two potential references . The programme states that contact information in the applicant s CV is sufficient for this purpose. Additional Documents for Successful Candidates Successful candidates will subsequently need to provide evidence of their institutional status. This includes: Proof of enrollment or employment Written permission from the employer if the applicant is employed The employer s written permission is required where applicable because the Next-Geo programme is an add-on programme alongside the participant s existing employment or academic affiliation. Application Deadline The deadline for applications that are guaranteed full consideration is October 31, 2026 . Applicants should prepare their CV, cover letter, one-page research project sketch, writing sample and two references well in advance of the deadline. Important Date Application Deadline: October 31, 2026 The organisers aim to finalise the selection of the 2027 cohort by the end of November 2026 . Read Full Details About This Opportunity And Apply HERE Why the Next-Geo Programme Is Relevant to Geoeconomics Researchers The programme brings together several components that are directly relevant to researchers seeking to develop expertise in geoeconomics. First, it provides specialised research training in a field where the programme identifies a shortage of systematic training. Second, it connects early-career researchers who may otherwise be working independently across different European institutions. Third, participants receive access to senior researchers and international experts who can provide feedback and mentoring. Fourth, the programme provides practical resources, including research assistant support and potential funding for data and AI subscriptions. Finally, it creates opportunities for participants to interact with policymakers, think tanks and practitioners and potentially present their research at an international conference. Research Support for Promising Projects One of the practical components of the programme is support for promising participant projects. Researchers may receive access to the programme s pool of student research assistants, while additional funding may be available for project-specific data and AI subscriptions. This can provide researchers with additional resources for conducting empirical analysis, gathering data, developing research outputs and advancing their projects during the programme year. The programme does not state that every participant will automatically receive all forms of research support. The call refers specifically to promising research projects as being eligible for such support. Research, Policy and Public Engagement Next-Geo extends beyond academic research training by incorporating policy engagement and public outreach. During the summer Research and Policy Workshop, participants interact with policymakers, think tanks and practitioners. The autumn conference also creates an opportunity for researchers to engage with an international expert audience and political decision-makers. This structure encourages participants to develop skills not only in conducting research but also in communicating research findings to audiences beyond academia.
